name: Paranasal implants

card.summary: Solid implants placed beside the base of the nose to fill paranasal hollowing and flatness, giving the midface more projection and a fuller profile.
card.note: Surgical procedure with risks including nerve, sinus and tear-duct complications; individual planning required.

quick.overview:
Paranasal implants are surgical implants placed on the bone beside the nose, in the area between the cheekbone and the upper lip. They add volume where the midface is flat or hollow.

The payoff is a more projected midface and a smoother profile. Studies are mostly case series and cohorts; one study of 33 patients found measurable soft-tissue change over the implant.
quick.how: A surgeon places a shaped implant, often porous polyethylene or patient-specific material, through an incision, sometimes alongside jaw surgery.
quick.risks: Reported complications include discomfort, sinusitis and tear-duct dysfunction that resolved after plate removal in one series. Forum users also discuss smile changes from over-projection.

lead: Paranasal implants, also called paranasal augmentation or midface implants, are solid implants placed on the bone beside the base of the nose, in the zone between the cheekbone, the nasal opening (piriform aperture) and the upper lip. They add volume where that area is flat or hollowed, which gives the midface more forward projection and a smoother, fuller line in profile and three-quarter view.[1][2][4]

Within looksmaxxing, paranasal flatness is classed as a skeletal (hardmaxx) feature. Threads on looksmax.org ask how to tell whether one has paranasal hollowing, share before-and-after results, compare implants with fillers and with Le Fort I osteotomy, and discuss how to match implant size to the cheek and paranasal area.[1][2][7][9][10][11][12] Posters usually describe the goal as a less sunken midface and a stronger "forward growth" look, while some raise concerns about how an implant changes the smile.[1][2]

In the surgical literature the same region is addressed in several ways: alloplastic implants such as porous polyethylene, patient-specific implants made from PMMA or PEEK, and bone-based corrections such as a modified Le Fort I step osteotomy. A 2016 study compared 33 patients who had 3 mm porous polyethylene paranasal augmentation with mandibular setback against 35 who had setback alone, measuring soft-tissue change on lateral cephalograms at 6 months.[3] Published reports are mostly small case series and technical notes rather than randomized trials.[4][5]

angle.text: The implant adds volume exactly where the paranasal area is flat, producing a more projected midface in profile.

paras: The paranasal area is the strip of midface that lies lateral to the nose, below the infraorbital rim and above the upper lip. In a well-projected midface the profile line runs smoothly from cheekbone through the nasal base to the lip; where the underlying maxilla is set back, that line looks concave. Surgeons describe this as paranasal flatness or concavity.[4][5]

Paranasal flatness is documented in maxillary deficiency with Class III malocclusion and in conditions such as unilateral cleft lip and palate, where a 2026 CBCT study of 30 patients measured the affected side about 3.8 mm further back than the unaffected side at the piriform aperture.[4][6] Residual concavity can also remain after Le Fort I advancement even when the teeth and jaws are well repositioned, which is why surgeons have described adding an implant in the same operation.[5][14]

Implants used in the wider cheek and midface include solid silicone, porous high-density polyethylene and ePTFE; the encyclopedic overview of cheek augmentation describes malar, submalar and combined shapes, an intraoral approach through the upper gum line as the usual route, and temporary sensation loss, asymmetry and infection among general risks.[17] Paranasal pieces are a smaller, more specialised variant and are often supplied as stock shapes or designed per patient.

Paranasal augmentation sits between facial implant surgery and orthognathic surgery, where surgeons look for ways to fill depressions that bone movements leave behind. The 2016 porous polyethylene study carried out paranasal augmentation alongside mandibular setback, a setting in which a flat midface can exaggerate the jaw's prominence.[3]

Online, the topic is concentrated on looksmax.org hardmaxx boards. Thread titles include general questions about who has had midface or paranasal implants, requests to identify paranasal flatness from photos, a thread calling paranasal hollowing an overlooked flaw, and posts sharing a female patient's result.[1][7][9][10][11][12] In one thread a poster questions whether a smiling woman in a photo has paranasal implants, prompting a debate over how such implants look in a smile.[13]

sections.h: How it is used to improve appearance
paras: The stated aim is volume and projection exactly where the profile is flat: the implant sits on the bone, the soft tissue drapes over it, and the nasal base and upper lip appear to sit more forward relative to the cheek. Community posters say this reduces a sunken or "recessed" midface look and balances the lower face against the eyes and cheekbones.[2][9]

Posters frame the decision against alternatives. Fillers are described as reversible and lighter-touch; Le Fort I osteotomy as a more invasive structural change that moves the whole upper jaw; implants as an intermediate, localized option.[2][15][17] One thread title refers to combining Le Fort 1, Le Fort 2, inframalar and paranasal implants in a theory of how to approach a recessed face.[16]

sections.h: Beliefs and claims in the community
paras: Forum users commonly say paranasal hollowing is easy to overlook because attention goes to the jaw and eyes, and that fixing it changes the whole midface read.[9] Others stress planning: a poster asks how to choose implant size for the cheek and paranasal region, and another warns that too much projection could affect the smile.[2][8] Some threads ask whether implants or a quadrangular Le Fort 1 give better results, with replies saying they face the same dilemma.[2]

A 24-patient case series of modified Le Fort I step osteotomy for paranasal flatness reported plate discomfort in two patients (8 percent), one with nasolacrimal duct dysfunction and occasional tearing that resolved after plate removal, and maxillary sinusitis in two patients (8 percent).[4]

Planning papers highlight nearby structures. A 2026 segmentation-based proof-of-concept study evaluated the anatomical eligibility of paranasal and transnasal implant sites in the atrophic maxilla with attention to the nasolacrimal duct, and the two-patient patient-specific PMMA report noted concerns about spatial conflict with fixation hardware and infraorbital nerve safety.[5][8] General cheek-implant risks listed by an encyclopedic summary include infection, bleeding, asymmetry, implant shift and sensation loss.[17]

Recent work concentrates on digital planning and patient-specific hardware. A 2026 finite element analysis tested a custom PEEK fixation plate designed to stabilize a Le Fort I-advanced maxilla while also restoring midfacial contour, reporting comparable stability to titanium fixation in the model.[14] The 2026 patient-specific PMMA report used 3D virtual planning so the implant shares the space with fixation plates.[5]

Human data are limited to small studies. The porous polyethylene comparison included 33 augmented patients and 35 controls with cephalometric soft-tissue measurements at 6 months and recorded complications and satisfaction.[3] The modified Le Fort I step osteotomy series (24 patients) reported a harmonious convex cheekbone-nasal base-lip contour in all patients and satisfaction with the aesthetic result.[4] Two patients with patient-specific PMMA implants combined with Le Fort I had satisfactory projection and no complications at 24 months.[5] No randomized trial of paranasal implants for purely cosmetic goals has been published.

timeline.event: Facial Plastic Surgery publishes a 33-patient comparison of 3 mm porous polyethylene paranasal augmentation with mandibular setback versus setback alone, with 6-month soft-tissue measurements.[3]
Technical note and 24-case series of modified Le Fort I step osteotomy for paranasal flatness published.[4]
looksmax.org threads compare paranasal implants with quadrangular Le Fort 1 for sunken midface, ask how to identify paranasal flatness, and request experiences with midface implants.[1][2][7]

Studies report CBCT quantification of paranasal asymmetry in cleft patients, a PEEK midface fixation model, a segmentation-assisted safety workflow and 2-year outcomes of patient-specific PMMA paranasal implants.[5][6][8][14]

lore.intro: Paranasal implants are discussed on looksmax.org hardmaxx boards as a targeted fix for sunken or flat midface, usually in comparison with fillers and Le Fort osteotomy.[1][2][9][12]

claims.claim: Implants versus Le Fort 1 for sunken midface
claims.believers: Posters ask whether a more invasive quadrangular Le Fort 1 gives better results than implants and what the difference is.[2]
claims.experts: A 24-patient series reports that a modified Le Fort I step osteotomy corrected paranasal flatness, while implant reports are mostly small cohorts.[3][4]

claims.claim: Paranasal hollowing is an overlooked flaw that changes the whole midface
claims.believers: A thread titled "paranasal hollowing is the most overlooked flaw" argues that the area matters more than commonly discussed.[9]
claims.experts: Surgical papers describe residual paranasal concavity as limiting the aesthetic impact of orthognathic surgery and as a target for augmentation.[5]

claims.claim: Too much projection can change the smile
claims.believers: Users warn that an oversized implant can alter how the smile looks; an original poster says the smile is their main worry.[1][2]
claims.experts: Published series focus on contour and complications such as plate discomfort and sinusitis; no study measures smile change.[3][4]

claims.claim: Implant size has to be matched to the individual
claims.believers: Threads ask how to choose the right size for cheek and paranasal implants.[8]
claims.experts: Reports increasingly use 3D virtual planning and patient-specific implants, with attention to nerve and tear-duct proximity.[5][8]

claims.claim: Fillers are a lighter option than implants
claims.believers: Forum threads compare implants and fillers for a recessed upper maxilla.[15]
claims.experts: A cheek augmentation overview describes hyaluronic acid filler as less invasive and temporary, and implants as permanent solids.[17]
